Honestly, it sucks. It's a decent enough game in its own right; not nearly worth the price or anyone's attention, but it should be shot for pretending to cater to the Dungeon Keeper crowd. That said, I guess it's okay if you pretend DK doesn't exist and this wasn't made to copy that much better series. title: Dark and Light
text: It seems ridiculous to write a review now for such an early EA. So this is more of  an account of my quite positive experience so far for anybody thinking about buying this game. To start with, DnL obviously uses ARK's core mechanics and menu/option layouts as one would expect, but I haven't gotten the impression that I'm playing ARK reskinned and I'll try and keep the ARK references to a minimum.  Currently I have 26 hours and a level 27 character (max character level is 60 (?), 120 for creatures) My specs :  Windows 10 64 bit, i7-4710 quadcore 2.5ghz, 8GB RAM, GTX 860M. This is early EA with all the problems that entails but I run the game in SP with absolutely minimal issues on med-high settings, it only stutters a little on map tile transitions. I've had no freezing, no CTDs or any noticeable serious graphical glitches or lag. LOAD TIMES are good once I get past the intial load which takes about 5-6 minutes. GRAPHICS are normal Unity engine quality. The ground is standard stuff, the ground clutter ,vegetation and rocks all look good and suit a fantasy continent although it does feel a little sparse a lot of the time, like all the little details are only 75% there. SOUND & MUSIC are currently minimal, but what there is of it is best desribed as adequate but not remarkable in any way. CHARACTER generation is quite good - instantly recognisable from ARK from which it borrows so many mechanics - but the characters have reasonable face customisation options and look very good in the generation window although they lose some of their crispness a little in game. CREATURES look good, original, move well, are plentiful (currently 150 apparently) and varied. AI and path finding generally seems to work quite well, they are very rarely stuck in trees or terrain, will hunt each other and may form packs (wolves/panthers) etc. Predators can at times just run in circles around you though doing no damage and making for an easy kill. Spawning has some issues (creature have occaisionally spawned immediately next to me), their 'I can see you and will attack' radius is insanely large and a few (panthers especially) seem OP near starting areas. You get camera shake when some of the bigger (eg Elemental) creatures are close by. Taming is also an option providing mounts (land and air) as well as harvesters/haulers. BIOMES I have visited only include beaches, forest, swamp, hills and mountains - all were adequate but not really amazingly different - the map assets changed so they look different but somehow the atmosphere felt largely the same. NPCs & CITIES - really enjoying this in SP , although obviously still a WIP, having vendors that buy and sell only limited item types and quantities works very well. Players can also upgrade them via donations to permanently improve their stocked items. The cities themselves are large (the human city has perhaps 80+ enterable buildings) and offer not only a safe haven but also various real estate options. Broader interaction with guards/citizens currently is non-existent and most buildings are still unfurnished. CHARACTER PROGRESSION is super and has 2 distinct halves. (1) Killing creatures and crafting things yields XP to level up which provides stat boosts (similar to ARK -str,stamina,hunger thirst etc but with a couple of extras). (2) Actions in game provide a percentage progression for related skills which all have ranks. EG - harvest plants by hand adds % to your Straw (Thatch) Building skill (which has 6 ranks with each rank providing extra building pieces), but harvest plants using a sickle adds to your farming skill and gives different resources from the same plants. The skill tree has about 30 core skills (farming, building, smelting, melee weapons, ranged weapons, armour, fire magic, air magic etc etc) with skills and ranks within those skills all unlocking only at certain levels. When you reach 100% on rank 1, if your level is high enough, you automatically become rank 2. This results is a slower more balanced power increase for characters where picking a lot of berries doesn't make you a good fighter. BUILDING is very ARK but with a few innovative pieces, eg dormer window rooves, Conan style triangular foundations and 2 types of doors. The system is currently not with out its faults (eg rotation is broken, terrain clipping, poor foundation height above ground) but the pieces look good and (a personal favourite) the inside of walls looks like the outside. Oh, and no pillar nipples :) SETTINGS can be tweaked, although not as extensively as ARK, but more than enough to eliminate any unwanted grind. Key rebinding works. MOVEMENT & COMBAT seem a little under-cooked ATM. Many slopes your granny could get up in a wheelchair will thwart your character forcing you to jump a lot or look for alternate paths. Combat is a bit of a 'swing wildly' approach and that will do the job, even if the beastie thing is behind you. Right clicking allows a slower but more powerful secondary attack with weapons that feels better and will often miss, overall combat is functional if not brilliant. Using magic for combat is satisfying but tricky on targets that move so quickly - a near miss with a fireball does no damage at all - and mana requirements mean spellcasting is not too OP, especially at low levels anyway. If I think of anything else to add I will do so later but generally for an EA this seems quite good when I think back to early EA ARK or the current mess that is Conan. In short, DnL works and it does what it does reasonably well, but currently without having an epic wow-factor (but then it is early EA and I am only 26 hours in game and still have much to discover). 7/10

title: DarkMaus
text: This is an astonishingly strong offering for a one-person team. It's less of a souls-like and more of a straight-up demake of Dark Souls, boiling it down into its most basic elements, with mice added in for flavor. The core elements of gameplay (skill-based combat, soft-capped stat-raising, equipment load, risk-vs-reward) are all center-stage and all feel great. Other elements (such as item-based lore, massive open world, complex NPC interactions) have been cut or minimized, and in some places the game feels a bit too pared-back because of it. The story in particular feels bare, although the overall atmosphere is intimate and oppressive enough to compensate for that. Similarly, encountering new enemies, new traps, new weapons, and new areas all feel great, even if there aren't a ton of those things overall. Ultimately, with the game being as short as it is (about 5 - 7 hours) it straddles the sweet spot between "this was just starting to get good" and "this was a perfectly bite-sized experience". Certain plot points come up, but are never fully fleshed out. The varied routes to the game's conclusion are mostly the same route with a few different flourishes. Implications about the broader world are made but not addressed. The whole thing practically begs for a feature-length sequel, although it's unclear if one is forthcoming. I would recommend this to a soulsborne purist without hesitation. For someone that likes the Souls games more for their lore than their gameplay, DarkMaus is either tantalizing with possiblity or a hopeless tease. For someone without any Soulslike experience, if you like highly techical games that reward you for careful play and good planning, and if you like to figure out how to play games as you play them, you'll enjoy this. If you like games that are easy or dialog-heavy or have AAA production values,you may want to look elsewhere. At full price, this is a reasonable buy, but on sale it's a steal. There's a lot of love put into this game, and it'll last you a solid few play sessions. Just bear in mind: there's no way to respec your stats, so pick either Strength or Skill for your primary weapon. Don't dump points into both.

title: Darkout
text: The first impression I had after looking at Darkout’s screenshots: it’s beautiful! Actually playing the game proved that screenshots didn’t lie: Darkout is by far the most beautiful game in 2D sandbox exploration/building genre, and while I believe that graphics isn’t that important, great graphics like this certainly adds to enjoyment. Graphics aside, Darkout has decent crafting and building system; there is a fair (but by no means spectacular) selection of decorative items to craft, and some interesting features, like research system or necessity to connect most advanced work stations to your base’s power grid. Overall, Darkout has interesting early to mid-game. Finding resources and progressing can be quite challenging, as even early enemies can be deadly when you are poorly equipped, and environment itself can present hazards like long falls or deadly tar pits. As you progress through the game, however, the challenge diminishes, not increases: while you start encountering stronger enemies, their strength increase doesn’t match your stronger weapons and armor, and eventually even hardest areas become a walk in a park with late-tier sword and armor. Aside from drastically diminishing challenge, as you keep playing you will eventually find Darkout rather lacking in variety: there are only 3 surface biomes, not counting very small and very empty coastline biome, and flying islands biome that looks the same as surface jungle biome (other than being composed of flying islands, naturally). There are several different underground layers, but only major difference between them is the music and what kinds of resources you can find there. Also, there is only one boss, and it can only be fought after a rather long questline. In the end, despite its flaws, Darkout is a good enough game, and if you are a fan of 2D sandbox exploration/building genre, Darkout will likely give you many hours of enjoyment.

text: As a developer I often see things that are obviously half-done and this, unfortunately, fits the bill.   The crafting is AMAZING and the world is absolutely beautiful, but story progression is a combination of tedium and luck with the Random Number Generator.   The devs are aware, but unfortnately, it leads to overcompensation and inventory bloat. The premise of this game is that you are a member of a colony ship, unfrozen and jettisoned onto the world below.  No-one above is aware of the catastrophic events that led them to stasis in that ship, and it's on you to find out why.  I think.   The problems with the story quickly crack open when early quests have you fetch broken parts of a beacon.  Pulling these into your inventory doesn't trigger anything; you then have to kill an enemy and get it to drop a log file (which could also be a blueprint or minor side story item).  This log will look and sound like it was intended to play when you found the broken beacon piece (which happens to also be a random drop from chests and crates that spawn in the wild). Once you've done this, the one voice acted character which isn't a computer but *is* interactive (sorta) grows ill in some way and bam, he's out of the story.  In fact, your entire beacon apparatus you spent tons of time building is also now just taking up space.  Hopefully by now you've been doing more things on your own and developing your base.  Enemies grow with your "Research Level" which is just your level, gained by mining and killing things and inventing. The story gets harder to follow; the concepts are more abstract and the only indicator as to where to kill something to get it to drop a log or data cube (and yes, this is how all story elements progress) is to catch the one hint in the last log as to where it will be found.   While I appreciate making exploration necessary to progress, this is overdone; there are gates you encounter that need "purification" later which require a lot of searching for some hard to find items (such as big stacks of a certain color of Crystal).   Furthermore, if you start "purifying" a gate you can't work any other gate until that specific one is fixed.  When you finally face a boss, it drops a "leet loot" item but fails to progress the story in any way I can see.  All of the logs that are "above" your spot in the plot line refuse to unlock so you can read them, and I now have 5 metal chests full and am filling a Vault (which holds 100 items). Some may say ripping on the acting in a game is nitpicky, but there is a limit to everything.   It's clear that someone from the sound studio must have quit their job during development; many of the audio clips have the actors rereading the line to deliver it how they want it to sound.  This normally doesn't make it past the sound studio; someone just grabbed the files and chucked them in.   You'll do a double-take the first time you read the line in the file, but hear the line spoken twice in a row with emphasis on different words.   Unfortunately, it does not have the endearing goof-up quality of the early days of TV like when Doctor Who had to be done in one take per scene. Still, I recommend a buy ON SALE.   The gameplay itself is pretty solid, outside of some graphics-lag issues when too many items you can't pick up are on screen (i.e. when inventory is full).   You'll get stuck in the story, however; it's essentially an endurance test to see if you will keep playing until you get lucky enough to progress the tale, or if you get bored and stop playing before then.   I regret to say, I am probably in the latter, as will most people be.

title: David.
text: In the span of an hour, I ripped through David. and saw every little oddity and battle offered. For many games I've played, it's a depressing detriment, and I crave more, but somehow the makers found a way to cram enjoyment and challenge without ever overstaying their welcome. Polished, gorgeous, and simple, and with a buttload of variety. The boss rush style set up can be make or break, but David. captures the excitement of high production fights with simple, genuinely fun boss fights that always bring something new to the table you have to adapt to. Going in, I played all the matches on the hardest difficulty, making it a one shot kill for me if I messed up or failed. In my humble opinion this is how the game was meant to be played, but regardless, there is a lot of reward to be had when clearing out a particularly difficult boss. Gameplay wise, you are a square that floats around and can blast the evil triangles away with your giant throbbing balls of light. It takes tact, understanding of the physics and decent aim. That's it. You will die. A lot. Few games do you learn from death so well, so expect a good challenge and a lovely, minimalistic abstract art style. For the miniscule price, David is worth the pennies. It sticks with you well after you finish, even though it doesn't have anything in particular to say. The music's also wonderful, so if you're looking for a great game that's off the beaten path, look no further.

text: David is a small, hollowed out square, with a special power. David contains several little ovals, which he can fling at enemies. He has been tasked with fighting and destroying evil, which he does by destroying 12 (very large) bosses. Presumably David's story is based on the biblical David, as you are a tiny hero taking on humongous foes, and the developer is quite clearly Christian (in addition to fighting sin, Jesus is the first thanked in his acknowledgements). The boss fights are fast-paced and frantic. They're also very challenging and often frustrating when playing on the high difficulty (which you have to do, in order to get to the final boss). After playing the first boss, you'd be forgiven for thinking that the game will become repetitive quickly, and while this is true to a certain extent, the bosses in David are actually fairly original and varied. There are an impressive array of novelties that make each boss fight unique and feel fresh. For example, in one of the bonus boss fights, your ellipsoidal ammunition no longer follows you, meaning you have to go to it, and fire it from where it lies. Little variations like this really keep the game fun. The downside is that this game is extremely short. Even with the arena mode, I would not expect more than a few hours. Five dollars is not an unreasonable asking price for something so different from the usual fare, but if you're uncertain, you can pick it up on sale. It is worth a try.

title: David.
text: David is a 2D arena shooter where you control a little floaty cube called David. David can slide from side to side and can jump repeatedly in mid-air, giving him a levitation ability but with a constant gravity pull. To attack an enemy, you click and hold on David to enter a slow-motion state where David charges his attack. His attack shoots a sphere in the direction you are pointing; this sphere being composed of smaller spheres that orbit David. How big your shot is depends on how many of the small spheres are within a certain boundary around David at the time you release the shot.  After firing, you need to wait for the spheres to come back to orbit around David before shooting again. The game has two modes. The main mode has you entering constrained arenas to fight bosses, and each boss has a certain gimmick that makes it unique. You will need to beat each boss twice, once with 7 hit points (easily managed) and 1 hit point (where the real fun is!). All the bosses are accessible at any time, except the final boss which requires that you successfully beat each minor boss at both difficulties. There is also an arena mode where enemies keep coming at you while you accumulate points. The points allow you to upgrade David to last longer in the next run. The game is definitely worth a purchase. It's a steal at $1, so get it while the offer lasts.
